disclosure.residualRisk: Two holders acting together can reach any record. That is a governance control rather than a cryptographic one, and it is why the shares sit in five organisations with different lines of accountability rather than with five people in one council. It is stated here, and in the threat model, rather than left for someone to discover.
disclosure.whyMeta: The part that makes the design lawful
disclosure.whyText: A system whose operator genuinely could not decrypt could not answer a subject access request, comply with a sheriff's order, or give the Care Inspectorate the access its scrutiny function requires. It would not be lawful to deploy. So the controller can always reach a record, and the question worth asking is not whether it can, but what it takes, who has to agree, and whether it is recorded. This screen is the answer to all three.

classifications.officialDefinition: The lowest classification, and the majority of information the public sector creates or processes, including routine business operations and services. Some of it could have damaging consequences if lost, stolen or published in the media, but it is not subject to a heightened risk profile. There is no requirement to explicitly mark routine Official information.
classifications.officialSensitiveDefinition: A limited subset of Official information that could have more damaging consequences if it were lost, stolen or published. It must be clearly marked Official-Sensitive, and special handling instructions may be added where the sensitivity justifies strict restrictions on sharing. Annex 2 gives four examples: case details involving vulnerable individuals where a serious risk of harm or criminal activity may result from disclosure; information about investigations, civil or criminal proceedings that could disrupt law enforcement or prejudice legal cases; security information; and personal data defined as special category or sensitive under data protection legislation.
classifications.scheme: All Scottish Government departments, non-departmental public bodies and agencies follow the UK Government Security Classification scheme, which has three levels: Official, Secret and Top Secret. Classifications indicate the sensitivity of information in terms of the likely impact of compromise, loss or misuse, and the need to defend against different threats. We each have a responsibility to protect and safeguard information.
classifications.secretDefinition: Very sensitive information that justifies heightened protective measures against determined and highly capable threats, where compromise could threaten life directly, seriously damage the United Kingdom's security or international relations, or seriously damage its financial security. Nothing in public protection casework reaches it, so this product never derives it.
classifications.topSecretDefinition: The most sensitive information, where compromise could cause widespread loss of life or threaten the security or economic wellbeing of the United Kingdom or its allies. Nothing in public protection casework reaches it, so this product never derives it.

accessRestriction.definition: Whether a record is reachable only by the people on it. It is a separate property from the classification, not a level of it: a MAPPA record is Official-Sensitive and access restricted, an adult protection case conference minute can be Official-Sensitive and not restricted, and an aggregate report is neither. The word appears in three unrelated senses in this product, so read carefully: this one is access to a record; a chronology event marked restricted is one that shows only to full-access members of a restricted process; and a restricted read in the audit log is a read of a restricted record, recorded separately so oversight can find it.

gsc.definition: Government Security Classification. The UK scheme every Scottish Government department, non-departmental public body and agency follows. It has three levels: Official, Secret and Top Secret. A classification says how sensitive information is in terms of the likely impact of its compromise, loss or misuse, and what it must be defended against. Only Official is reachable in this product, with the Official-Sensitive marking on the subset that needs it: nothing in public protection casework reaches defence, diplomacy or national security.

official.definition: The lowest Government Security Classification, and the majority of what the public sector creates or processes. Some of it could have damaging consequences if lost, stolen or published, but it is not subject to a heightened risk profile. There is no requirement to mark routine Official information, and this product does not mark it: a product that stamps every page trains people to ignore markings.

officialSensitive.definition: A limited subset of Official information that could have more damaging consequences if lost, stolen or published. It must be clearly marked, and special handling instructions may be added where the sensitivity justifies strict restrictions on sharing. Annex 2 of the MAPPA National Guidance gives four examples: case details involving vulnerable individuals where a serious risk of harm or criminal activity may result from disclosure; information about investigations or proceedings that could disrupt law enforcement or prejudice a case; security information; and personal data defined as special category or sensitive under data protection legislation.

restrictedTerm.definition: RESTRICTED was a level of the old Government Protective Marking Scheme and was abolished on 2 April 2014, when the six-tier scheme (Unclassified, Protect, Restricted, Confidential, Secret, Top Secret) was replaced by the three-level Government Security Classification scheme. Official absorbed everything up to and including it, and there is no direct mapping between the two schemes. This product does not use it as a classification, and any document that still does is working to a scheme that has been gone for over a decade.

browser.text: On the desktop application your key is held by the operating system's own keychain, tied to your account on that machine and, on most computers, to the hardware. A web browser has nothing equivalent, so in a browser the key sits in the page's storage, where any script running on the page could read it, and with it every case cached on that device. That is a different kind of risk rather than a smaller one, so the desktop application is the supported way to use this and the browser build is for development and for demonstrations. If your organisation does allow browser access, treat any cross-site scripting fault in the application as a key compromise: revoke the device, do not simply refresh the page.
browser.title: Why the desktop application rather than a browser

colleagues.text: No. Encryption controls who can open a record; it cannot control what someone does with a record they are entitled to open. Someone on a case sees the case. What the product does instead is record every read, record every restricted read separately, and make the audit log impossible to edit quietly, so misuse is found afterwards rather than prevented beforehand. If someone tells you encryption solves this, they are selling something.
colleagues.title: Does this stop a colleague misusing a case they are on

escrow.meta: Yes, and it has to be able to
escrow.text: Yes, through escrow, and this is deliberate. The council is the data controller and has to be able to answer a subject access request, comply with a sheriff's order, and give the Care Inspectorate the access its scrutiny function requires. A system that genuinely could not do those things would not be lawful to run. What makes it safe is that no one person can do it: the escrow key is split five ways across five different organisations, and reaching a record needs two of them acting together, from different organisations, with a recorded reason and lawful basis. Both sign the record of it, the other three are told it happened, and it appears in the audit log. The honest limit is that two holders acting together can reach anything, which is why they sit in five organisations with different lines of accountability rather than five people in one building.
escrow.title: So can the council ever get at a record

lostKey.meta: They are working again within the hour
lostKey.text: Revoke the device from Settings, which anyone can do for their own devices immediately, and enrol a replacement. Enrolling needs either another device you already have or two colleagues approving, and the approver reads a short code back to you so an enrolment cannot be quietly redirected to somebody else's machine. Your keys are then restored through the same escrow path, with your identity checked and the whole thing recorded. This is tested, because an untested recovery path is the usual way an encrypted system ends up unusable, and a practitioner who cannot open a safety plan is a safeguarding problem rather than an IT one.
lostKey.title: What happens if someone loses their laptop

offline.text: Cases you already have stay open. Your keys for them are held on the device and keep working for three days by default, so a duty worker at three in the morning on a bank holiday is not stopped by a server they cannot reach. The status bar shows how long is left once the clock is running. Being added to a new case does need a connection, and the product says so at the point it matters rather than showing you an empty record.
offline.title: What happens out of hours, or with no signal

search.meta: The cost of the design, stated
search.text: A system that cannot read your records cannot build an index of them, so search runs on your own device instead. When you sign in, the records you are entitled to are decrypted locally and indexed in memory. One consequence is worth knowing: search covers what you can see and nothing else, so a record you are not on will not appear even if you search for exactly the right thing. The screen says how many records were not searched, so you can tell the difference between "there is nothing" and "there is nothing you can see".
search.title: Why search works differently here

whatIsEncrypted.meta: The one place the phrase is exact
whatIsEncrypted.text: Record content is end-to-end encrypted. Every record is encrypted on the device that writes it, under a key of its own, and that key is wrapped only to the people the need-to-know rules entitle. Nobody else holds anything that opens it, including whoever hosts the system. That is not a permission a server chooses to honour, it is a fact about who holds which key: a colleague who is not on a case has nothing to try, so there is nothing to look up. That is the most common breach in this sector, and this is what turns it from something audit catches afterwards into something that cannot happen.
whatIsEncrypted.title: What is encrypted

whatIsNot.meta: Said plainly, because a half-answer here is worse than none
whatIsNot.text: The product as a whole is not end-to-end encrypted, and you should not say it is. Three things are deliberately readable. Metadata: whoever runs the system can see that a record exists, roughly what kind it is, what classification it carries, roughly when it was worked on, and how many people hold a key. Not who they are, not the person's name, not a word of the content. The audit log: who did what, to which record, when, all readable, because it exists to be read by a Caldicott guardian, a lead officer, an inspector or the ICO, and encrypting it to the people it polices would be backwards. Only the free-text detail in an entry is encrypted. And search: what you type never leaves your device, but a small number of exact-match lookups use a tag that lets the system tell that two records share a value without knowing what the value is.
whatIsNot.title: What is not encrypted

whoCanSee.meta: Nobody, and there is a screen that shows it
whoCanSee.text: Nobody hosting or administering the system holds a key that opens a record. There is no master key and no administrative override. If you want to see this rather than take it on trust, Admin has a screen called "What the host can see": it renders the store exactly as a hosting provider or a database administrator would see it, beside the same record as you see it. Both panels read the same store. The difference is a key.
whoCanSee.title: Who at the supplier can see our records

caveats.caring: Caring responsibilities and the presence of a child at an incident are not recorded as fields, so indicator 18 is returned as nought throughout. The nought means not collected, not none.
caveats.ethnicity: Ethnicity is not held in this system, so all {count} categories are returned as nought. The nought means not collected rather than none: no adult declined to answer, because the question is not asked.
caveats.gender: Gender is derived from the sex held on the record, so only Male and Female carry figures. Trans or non-binary and Prefer not to say are returned as nought because the question is not asked, not because nobody answered that way.
caveats.orderDates: Protection orders carry no date of their own on the record, so each is counted in the quarter its inquiry was triggered in. Where a case runs across a quarter boundary this can place an application a quarter early.
caveats.synthetic: Figures cover {from} to {to}. This return was prepared from a demonstration dataset and contains no real case information.
caveats.uptake: Uptake is left blank where no invitation was issued in the quarter. Nought per cent would read as a failure to invite anyone, which is a different thing from having nobody to invite.
